 Wall Street ends sharply lower on AI jitters ahead of Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO
 A ticker shows Nvidia trades as futures-options traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange's NYSE American (AMEX) in New York City, US, Nov 13, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Brendan McDermid)

 NEW YORK: A broad selloff dragged US stocks lower on Monday (Nov 16) as fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO soured enthusiasm for AI stocks , raising the stakes for the chipmaker's earnings report on Tuesday and Anthropic's initial public offering later in the week.
 The risk-off sentiment gathered momentum as the session progressed, with the S&P 500 dropping nearly 2 per cent and the Dow falling more than 1.4 per cent. The Nasdaq suffered the steepest percentage loss, tumbling 2.5 per cent, as the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index weighed on the tech-heavy index. The SOX lost 5.3 per cent.
 "It's the back-and-forth in this market of the AI-related stocks catching a bid versus this rotation trade," said Ross Mayfield, investment strategy analyst at Baird in Louisville, Kentucky. "Over the last couple of weeks, it's like a day-to-day thing where, you know, some days the AI names absolutely rip and then the very next day, you know, they're in a freefall."
 "There are signs underneath the surface that investors aren't panic-selling and running away from the asset class altogether, but are probing other corners of the equity market," Mayfield added.

 Nvidia slid 4.1 per cent, extending its losses after Huang's resignation following allegations of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, adding to concerns over the emerging technology's rapid expansion and potential risks.
 Huang's departure prompted the Trump administration to issue a new rule restricting China's access to the best AI chips from companies like Nvidia ahead of US President Donald Trump's expected meeting with his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping.
 Related: 
 Trump says 'would not mind' Huang being reinstated at Nvidia 
 US to curb China's access to AI chips as Trump heads to Asia 
 It marks an abrupt reversal of fortune for the sector. In mid-June the SOX index was up 106.6 per cent year-to-date. But that luster has faded in recent months, reducing its 2026 gain to around 43 per cent, still about four times the gains of the broader S&P 500 so far this year.
 That retreat helped pull the Nasdaq more than 10 per cent below its all-time closing high reached on October 6, confirming the index is in a correction.
 Analysts expect Nvidia to post a 90.4 per cent year-on-year earnings jump on revenue of US$109.10 billion.
 The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739.38 points, or 1.41 per cent, to 51,608.17, the S&P 500 .SPX lost 145.08 points, or 1.92 per cent, to 7,416.59 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 626.51 points, or 2.49 per cent, to 24,509.76.
 WARSH REMARKS, RATE-HIKE PROBABILITY 
 US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said on Monday that technologies will have a significant impact on the economy, but the possible scenarios range from rising growth with broadly shared gains to higher unemployment and a potential slowdown if anticipated investment returns prove disappointing.
 Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's latest meeting, due for release on Wednesday, could offer clues on the policy outlook ahead of next month's interest-rate decision.
